headline: Canada announces new tariffs on US goods

sources.title: As Canada readies retaliatory tariffs, Mark Carney says his nation is 'at war' with U.S. (NPR)
Canada to hit US with retaliatory tariffs as trade war escalates (Al Jazeera)
Canada announces retaliatory tariffs against the U.S. (PBS NewsHour)
Canada announces retaliatory tariffs on US goods (video, Reuters)

chunks.text: Canada has announced new [[tariffs]] on American goods in a [[trade dispute]] with the United States. Trade talks {{broke down}} on August 22, and the US then {{put on}} a 50 percent tariff covering about 20 billion dollars' [[worth of]] Canadian goods, including [[dairy]] and hockey equipment. Those goods {{make up}} about 5.5 percent of Canada's [[exports]] to the US. On August 25, 2026, Prime Minister Mark Carney {{laid out}} Canada's answer: it is {{striking back}} with tariffs of its own.

verbs.correct: To fail or end without agreement
verbs.wrong: To make sudden progress after difficulty
verbs.why: Peace talks can break down over one small detail, and a deal between a landlord and a tenant can break down over money. Trade talks between Canada and the United States broke down on August 22, three days before Canada's announcement.

verbs.correct: To make goods subject to a tax
verbs.wrong: To remove a tax from goods
verbs.why: A city can put a tax on sugary drinks, and a landlord can put a fee on late rent. After the talks ended, the United States put a 50 percent tariff on about 20 billion dollars' worth of Canadian goods.

verbs.correct: To form a part of a total
verbs.wrong: To send goods to another country
verbs.why: Women make up half of the company's staff, and rent makes up most of my monthly budget. The goods hit by the American tariffs make up about 5.5 percent of Canada's total exports to the US.

verbs.wrong: To cancel a plan at the last minute
verbs.why: A coach lays out the game plan before kickoff, and a teacher lays out the rules on the first day of class. Prime Minister Mark Carney laid out Canada's answer on August 25: tariffs of its own.

verbs.correct: To respond to an attack with your own
verbs.wrong: To cancel a law or rule in court
verbs.why: A boxer strikes back after taking a punch, and a team strikes back with a goal of its own after falling behind. Canada is now striking back at the American tariffs with tariffs of its own.

chunks.text: Carney said Canada would [[match]] the American tariffs "[[dollar for dollar]] in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses." Canada's tariffs {{add up to}} about 20 billion dollars, at rates of 15 to 50 percent. The new [[measures]] {{single out}} steel and aluminum for the largest share. The list includes cheese and other dairy, [[appliances]], farm equipment, seafood, [[cosmetics]], toilet paper, and electronics. Canadian tariffs on American auto parts [[remain in place]].

verbs.why: Small daily coffees add up to a big bill by the end of the month, and three short drives add up to a full tank of gas. Canada's new tariffs add up to about 20 billion dollars, the same amount as the American ones.

verbs.correct: To choose one thing for special treatment
verbs.wrong: To put products into groups by type
verbs.why: A coach singles out one player for praise, and a teacher singles out a student who needs extra help. The new measures single out steel and aluminum for the largest share of the tariffs.

chunks.text: Carney explained why the [[negotiations]] failed: "We learned during the negotiations that the Americans want to destroy our major industries, including autos, steel and aluminum." He {{summed up}} the dispute [[in blunt terms]]: "You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked." A [[poll]] by Leger found that 56 percent of Canadians favored a [[hardline approach]] with no further [[concessions]] to the US. Most did not want their government to {{back down}}.

verbs.correct: To state the main point in a few words
verbs.wrong: To count the money that was spent
verbs.why: A good speaker sums up a long talk in one sentence, and a report ends by summing up the key facts. Carney summed up the dispute in blunt terms, saying Canada was at war because it had been attacked.

verbs.correct: To drop your demands under pressure
verbs.wrong: To give support to someone's claim
verbs.why: A boss may back down after the whole team complains, and a customer backs down when the store shows the receipt. Most Canadians in the Leger poll did not want their government to back down or make more concessions.

chunks.text: Canada has also {{set aside}} about 7.5 billion Canadian dollars, or roughly 5.4 billion US dollars, for a [[support package]] for workers and businesses. Reports on the [[trade war]] warn that tariffs could {{push up}} prices, cost jobs, and leave [[small and medium-sized businesses]] at risk. Some could {{go under}} if the dispute {{drags on}}. It is unclear whether the two sides can {{work out}} a deal before Canada's tariffs [[take effect]] on September 8.

verbs.correct: To keep money for a special purpose
verbs.wrong: To make progress slower or later
verbs.why: Families set aside money for a summer vacation, and a school sets aside part of its budget for new books. The Canadian government has set aside about 7.5 billion Canadian dollars to support workers and businesses hurt by the dispute.

verbs.correct: To make prices or costs higher
verbs.wrong: To force a plan to be approved
verbs.why: A hot summer pushes up the price of ice, and high rents push up the cost of running a shop. Tariffs on both sides could push up costs and prices for people in both countries.

verbs.correct: To fail as a business and close
verbs.why: A restaurant can go under after one bad winter, and a small shop goes under when a big store opens next door. Some small and medium-sized businesses could go under if the trade dispute drags on.

verbs.wrong: To involve someone in a problem
verbs.why: A boring meeting drags on all afternoon, and a court case can drag on for years. Small businesses are at risk if the tariff dispute drags on for months.

verbs.correct: To reach an agreement by talking
verbs.why: Roommates work out who pays for what, and a couple works out a schedule for the kids. It is not yet clear whether the two governments will work out a new agreement before September 8.

mainIdea.s: After talks with the United States failed, Canada announced tariffs on 20 billion dollars of American goods. The prime minister says the move matches the US tariffs and protects Canadian workers.
mainIdea.why: Talks broke down on August 22, the United States put 50 percent tariffs on Canadian goods, and Carney answered with matching tariffs to protect Canadian workers.

mainIdea.s: Canada acted first with tariffs on American goods, and the United States then answered with 50 percent tariffs. Canadian officials say the goal is to protect workers, farmers, and businesses.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the United States acted first. Canada announced its tariffs on August 25 in response to the American tariffs that followed the failed talks.

mainIdea.s: The United States and Canada have signed a trade deal that removes most tariffs on steel and aluminum. Officials say it will take effect next year once lawmakers in both countries approve it.
mainIdea.why: There is no new trade deal. Talks broke down on August 22, and both countries are adding tariffs, not removing them.

tf.s: The United States put tariffs of 15 percent on Canadian goods.
tf.why: The United States put a 50 percent tariff, not a 15 percent one, on about 20 billion dollars' worth of Canadian goods after the talks broke down.

tf.s: Steel and aluminum make up the largest share of Canada's new measures.
tf.why: Steel and aluminum get the largest share, with dairy, appliances, farm equipment, seafood, and electronics also on the list.

tf.s: Most Canadians polled want Canada to make more concessions.
tf.why: The poll found that 56 percent of Canadians favored a hardline approach with no further concessions. Most did not want the government to back down.

tf.s: Canada's new tariffs take effect on September 8, 2026.
tf.why: Carney laid out the plan on August 25, 2026, and the tariffs take effect two weeks later, on September 8.

tf.s: Canada set aside about 20 billion dollars for its support package.
tf.why: The support package is worth about 7.5 billion Canadian dollars, or roughly 5.4 billion US dollars.

tf.s: Canada's tariffs add up to about 20 billion dollars.
tf.why: Canada's tariffs total about 20 billion dollars, matching the American tariffs dollar for dollar.

lines.text: Did you see the news? Canada is {{striking back}} with tariffs on American goods.
[[So much for]] the trade talks. I thought both sides were still at the table.
Not anymore. The talks {{broke down}} on August 22. Then the US {{put a 50 percent tariff on}} Canadian goods, and now Canada is doing the same.
That's a lot of money. Twenty billion dollars, right?
Yes, dollar for dollar. Steel and aluminum are the biggest part, but the list {{adds up to}} way more than that. Cheese, furniture, even toilet paper.
Toilet paper, [[of all things]]? What else is on there?
Cosmetics, appliances, seafood, electronics. And all of it will probably {{push up}} prices on both sides of the border.
So [[where does that leave]] regular people?
[[Caught in the middle]]. The government {{set aside}} some money to help businesses, but small companies could still {{go under}} if this {{drags on}}.
Do you think either side will {{back down}}?
[[Somebody has to blink first]]. But a poll found most Canadians don't want their government to make more concessions.
I hope they {{work out}} something before September 8.
[[I wouldn't hold my breath]]. That's not much time.

expressions.def: Used when a plan or hope has clearly failed or ended
ex: It's raining again. So much for our picnic.
So much for the diet. He ordered dessert.

expressions.def: Used to show surprise that something unexpected is included
ex: She brought a ladder, of all things, to the party.
He collects old phone books, of all things.

expressions.def: Used to ask what the situation now means for someone
ex: The bus route was cut, so where does that leave people without a car?
If the factory closes, where does that leave the workers?

expressions.def: Stuck between two sides in a fight and hurt by both
ex: When the neighbors argued, the kids were caught in the middle.
Small shops are caught in the middle when big suppliers raise prices.

expressions.def: Used when two sides refuse to give in and one will have to change first
ex: The strike is in its third week. Somebody has to blink first.
They both want the last word, but somebody has to blink first.

expressions.def: Used to say you do not expect something to happen soon
ex: He said he'd pay me back, but I wouldn't hold my breath.
A new train line by next year? I wouldn't hold my breath.
